articles.title: ChatGPT update adds Apple Messages integration on Mac
articles.subtitle: Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The new Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search chats on a Mac, and prepare and send messages. OpenAI says it is available across all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, with support in both ChatGPT Work and Codex.

That access raises privacy and control questions, so OpenAI stresses that sending remains gated by user approval under the default settings. Users should take care before granting persistent approval. OpenAI’s plugin guide details the risks, how to revoke access, and a known issue involving tasks that disable approval prompts.

We've added native integration with iMessage, so ChatGPT can now send & read messages for you! It can also analyze your messages! It's really fun to get insights about who you talk to, and what you talk to people about. https://t.co/OBIH5H3z6b pic.twitter.com/W0f6htZKvL — Ari Weinstein (@AriX) August 20, 2026

We've added native integration with iMessage, so ChatGPT can now send & read messages for you! It can also analyze your messages! It's really fun to get insights about who you talk to, and what you talk to people about. https://t.co/OBIH5H3z6b pic.twitter.com/W0f6htZKvL

Here’s more from the release notes:

Use the Apple Messages plugin to read and search Messages chats on your Mac and prepare or send messages. It’s available on all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS. You can use the plugin in ChatGPT Work and Codex. By default, ChatGPT sends messages only after you approve the message and its recipients. See the plugin guide for persistent-approval risks, revocation steps, and the known issue with tasks that disable approval prompts.

Separately, OpenAI details how the Messages feature works on its dedicated plugin site:

The Apple Messages plugin is available on all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS. In Codex and ChatGPT Work, it can read and search iMessage, SMS, and RCS chats on your Mac and send messages on your behalf through the Messages app. It doesn’t let you interact with ChatGPT remotely through Messages, and it doesn’t work in regular ChatGPT chats.

For now, the feature only works with ChatGPT on Apple silicon Macs and not Intel machines.

If you do ask ChatGPT to send a message on your behalf, it prompts for confirmation before anything is sent. Optionally, you can choose to skip the confirmation on a per-conversation basis.

Looking for the new feature inside ChatGPT? This link should go directly to the Messages plugin for ChatGPT on the Mac.

(taps dictation) 🗣️ “hey Codex, check my inbox and clean up those spam messages for me, please” https://t.co/VIttDr0aj3 pic.twitter.com/42IxeWbdHh — Victor E. Nunez (@victornunez) August 20, 2026

(taps dictation) 🗣️ “hey Codex, check my inbox and clean up those spam messages for me, please” https://t.co/VIttDr0aj3 pic.twitter.com/42IxeWbdHh

Site co-editing, shared thread snapshots, and more

While the Messages plugin is the standout addition for Apple users, the release includes several other improvements. For example, pinned chats now stay in sync across the ChatGPT desktop app and iOS, so users can keep important conversations accessible between a Mac and iPhone.

ChatGPT also now lets users share a read-only snapshot of a local Codex thread. These snapshots do not change as the original thread evolves.

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: PSA: In the latest GTA 6 leak's aftermath, it's not a good idea to download files with names like totallylegitgta6leakedbuild.exe
articles.subtitle: Also beware anything dubbed certainlynotavirusthisisgta6myboy.exe While scammers and other ne'er-do-wells leaning into the allure of playing GTA 6 as part of their efforts to spread malware isn't anything new - cybersecurity companies have been issuing...
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Also beware anything dubbed certainlynotavirusthisisgta6myboy.exe

While scammers and other ne'er-do-wells leaning into the allure of playing GTA 6 as part of their efforts to spread malware isn't anything new - cybersecurity companies have been issuing warnings about it for months - there appears to have been an uptick in such behaviour following the latest GTA 6 leak. With speculation rampant as to what exactly the hackers known as Cyberleek may have access to, now is not the time to be downloading any files claiming to be GTA 6.

Users on ResetEra and VPN service NordVPN, the latter of whom obviously have a vested interest in convincing people to think about taking more action to secure their PCs and browsing, claim to have observed an uptick in download links to alleged GTA 6 builds on piracy and torrenting sites.

These new links are alleged to be trying to pass themselves off as being from Cyberleek, as a means to try and trick people into downloading malware that's slightly less obvious than just declaring 'omg, here's random early access to GTA 6' as many seemed to have been doing to this point.

Because misinformation just piles atop misinformation nowadays, it also appears one of the alleged dodgy GTA 6 leaked build listings being circulated on social media could just be a faked screenshot.

You probably don't need to be told this, but it'd be very stupid to try and download an alleged version of GTA 6 from some rando on the internet.

I'm writing that anyway because, as the game's console launch on November 19th looms with no news yet of a PC launch, this sort of thing is likely only going to become more widespread in the coming months. Not necessarily a problem for the fairly tech-savvy, as I'd assume the typical reader of a gaming site to be, but possibly more of a risk to kids and older folks who might be asked by such kids for a copy of GTA 6.

So, it's maybe worth bearing in mind and warning any relatives or friends you reckon might be at risk of dodgy GTA 6 downloads next time you see them. After all, once the game's out on consoles, it could get a bit tougher to tell the legit from the bogus for those not keeping up with news of which platforms the game's available on.

The next official look at GTA 6 is set to premiere on Netflix on August 27th, hitting YouTube a few hours later. Meanwhile, next month will see 34 former Rockstar devs' legal battle against the studio over their firings last year reach its final trial.

articles.title: Open and move windows between displays automatically
articles.subtitle: When I was visiting my pal Myke Hurley in London last year, I noticed that he had a second display to the right of his main one.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
When I was visiting my pal Myke Hurley in London last year, I noticed that he had a second display to the right of his main one. It was large and mounted vertically, and when he recorded a podcast, he kept all his recording information over there. I liked the idea of monitoring my recordings while they were going on, just for extra peace of mind, and a second display seemed like the right way to do it.

If only I had a second display! But I do, of course, because my main Mac is now a MacBook Pro. So I’ve taken to recording podcasts using the “Hurley Method,” with my Audio Hijack windows positioned on the laptop display, off to my left.

It’s nice, but if you know me, I quickly became frustrated by the number of clicks and drags I needed to perform every single time I record a podcast: Open up my laptop, open Audio Hijack, open the list of recording sessions, double-click on the one I’m using right now, then drag the window over to the laptop display.

So today I automated it.

None of my automations work if I haven’t opened the laptop, and while it sits next to my Mac in a nice stand from Twelve South, it’s closed most of the time. So my first step before moving windows to the laptop display is to make sure that the display is available! Fortunately, there’s a command-line command for that:

If you want, you can simplify the output by piping it through a grep command like system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType | grep -B1 "Resolution", but all I really want to do is search for the text string “Built-in”, which indicates that the laptop is open and its built-in display is running.

I automate most of my recording stuff using Keyboard Maestro macros triggered by an Elgato Stream Deck. So I built my automation into an existing macro in Keyboard Maestro, just adding a new if/then statement: If the calculation `SCREENCOUNT() > 1 returns true.

Then the macro runs the shell script, saves that to a local variable called LocalScreens, and it’s time for one more if/then statement, to ensure that this part of the macro only runs when more than one screen is attached and when the internal MacBook Pro display is active.

Unfortunately, the next step requires automating Audio Hijack, and while that app is very scriptable via JavaScript, and controllable via Shortcuts (or a plain text file?!), there’s no direct method of automating it from within Keyboard Maestro. So I created a basic Shortcut containing the JavaScript required to tell Audio Hijack to open a specific session by name, with the name passed to the Shortcut as input:

Then it’s a one-step item in Keyboard Maestro to run that shortcut with the name of my Audio Hijack session as the input:

(I wish this was cleaner and I didn’t need to run a shortcut. The alternative is to literally write out a text file containing the JavaScript and run it via a shell script. Is that cleaner? Doesn’t feel like it, but it’s more self-contained and doesn’t rely on the good graces of Shortcuts.)

Now that I know that my MacBook Pro display is open and my Audio Hijack session window is open, it’s a one-step command in Keyboard Maestro to make the move:

This one’s a little tricky. I have to use the Move and Resize Window command, but instead of standard numerical values, I need to use custom “smart” values that Keyboard Maestro supports.

In this case, horizontally it’s SCREENVISIBLE(Internal,MidX)-600 —essentially, 600 pixels to the left of the midpoint of the internal display—and vertically it’s SCREENVISIBLE(Internal,MidY)-250 —250 pixels up from the midpoint of the display. You can play around with the dimensions until the window ends up in the right spot, and of course, at the right size.

And that was it. Now, when I press my recording button on my Stream Deck, if my laptop display is open, the session window will automatically pop open on my laptop display. I sure do like it when things happen on my computer automatically.

articles.title: Meta AI is now available as a more capable desktop app for Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI. Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI.

Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.

Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app.

Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Beyond chat, the sidebar includes Media, Artifacts, scheduled tasks, conversation history, and an “About Me” personalization section.

Users can switch among thinking modes, attach files, generate media, and create recurring briefings or reminders. The app also includes the ability to hide the Dock icon, allowing it to be invoked with a keyboard shortcut instead.

Meta’s recent AI push

The Mac app is the latest in a steady run of releases. In April, Meta replaced Llama with Muse Spark. A May update then expanded Meta AI with more natural voice conversations and live camera-based assistance.

July brought Muse-powered image generation to Meta AI, WhatsApp, and Instagram, although Meta quickly removed one feature that generated images from public Instagram posts. Meta AI also moved into Threads DMs for private chats.

Most recently, Meta launched Muse Code, a terminal-based AI coding agent for macOS and Linux.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: I've just finished reviewing AMD's latest gaming CPU and I would genuinely considering switching back to Intel
articles.subtitle: It's not that the 7700X3D is a bad chip, but the value proposition of Intel's CPUs is mighty tempting for a budget gamer.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
I'll get it clear right out of the gate: I think the AMD 3D V-Cache chips are absolutely the best choice for a PC gamer wanting to get the absolute most out of their system when it comes purely to silky gaming frame rates. They're great CPUs, which use a hefty dollop of extra L3 cache specifically to improve their gaming performance, and that's why the Ryzen 7 9800X3D still sits proudly at the top of our best CPU for gaming list.

But, having just finished writing up my AMD Ryzen 7 7700X3D review, AMD's latest pitch for a budget gaming chip, it's made me seriously consider whether I would actually pick Intel's Core Ultra 5 250K Plus instead. And I rather think I might.

The whole justification for the existence of the 7700X3D—a chip that is essentially just a slower clocked Ryzen 7 7800X3D, itself a great CPU from 2023—is that AMD is delivering a more affordable 3D V-Cache CPU to drop into your existing AM5 motherboard. That is, on the surface, a laudable endeavour.

There are a couple of problems here, however. The first is competition from within the AMD stables; namely the fact that, while the 7700X3D does have a vastly lower MSRP to that of the 7800X3D (it's $329 plays $450) the older chip has had a long time to establish itself in retail and as such there are a lot of them around. And that means the actual on-sale prices are essentially the same, and sometimes the 7800X3D is actually available for less than the 7700X3D.

And the second issue is that the value proposition of the 7700X3D only really stands up if you are looking to make a CPU upgrade to an existing AM5 system. Say, if you've already got a rig with a Ryzen 5 7600 in it, for example. But if you're building a new system from scratch—and if you are, I feel your pricing pain, my droog—then at this end of the market the latest Intel Arrow Lake chips are mighty tempting.

The Intel Core Ultra 5 250K Plus has popped up with low-end pricing and high-end performance. It may only come rocking a six Performance-core layout, with 12 Efficient-cores, but that does give it 18 cores of multi-threaded grunt and some surprisingly good gaming prowess to boot.

1080p gaming performance

We test games at 1080p for CPU tests to better highlight performance diffences between chips

Synthetic gaming performance

The industry standard 3DMark benchmark is a good measure of relative capabilities even if it doesn't necessarily translate into gaming performance

Sure, it's not quite got the 3D V-Cache boost, but in a lot of games the Intel chip is really not far off the pace of either the 7700X3D or the 7800X3D. And it comes with a price tag of just $200. Even AMD's budget six-core X3D chip, the Ryzen 5 7600X3D is more expensive than that.

Intel's chip will give you a far more rounded processor, with plenty of gaming and a ton of productivity performance for $130 less than the latest X3D budget option. That gives you $130 dollars to spend on a better GPU than you might have otherwise been able to afford if you'd built around the AMD platform. And just look at the relative compute power on offer with this thing versus the more expensive AMD chips.

Compute performance

We may be PC Gamer but we also want to know what the productivity capabilities are of our CPUs

The caveat to the Intel positivity here, though, is the platform longevity of AMD's AM5 socket is absolutely unrivalled in the industry. While AMD has confirmed that it will be supporting the socket through to 2029, and has recently celebrated the 10 year lifespan (and counting) of its AM4 platform, Intel is still replacing its CPU socket pretty much every generation.

So yes, that means the board you stick the Core Ultra 5 250K Plus into only has a very limited upgrade path within the Arrow Lake generation, and any new Intel chips you covet will require an entire motherboard upgrade, too. That means, if you are the sort of person who is going to look at a CPU upgrade down the line, the dead-end of the Intel LGA 1851 socket is going to be a barrier to your future-proofing plans.

But it's worth asking yourself whether that really is going to be you. Be honest. When was the last time you actually did an in-place CPU upgrade? The notion of future-proofing your build with an easy upgrade path is always a tempting one, and is a good way to extend the operating life of your rig, especially in these 'spensive times of ours.

But if you're one of the majority of PC gamers who never touches that part of your machine, who might only ever upgrade their GPU or SSD at a push, then maybe it's worth considering making the savings up front and putting that towards a better graphics card in your build.

Apple Music will soon show a “Made With AI” label on music that was materially generated using artificial intelligence, giving listeners a clear indication when generative AI played a significant role in creating a song or other content. Apple has informed music industry partners that the labels will arrive later this year, although the company has not announced a specific launch date.

The Hollywood Reporter obtained an email Apple sent to industry partners on Thursday, which says content providers must use AI Transparency Tags whenever AI created a material portion of submitted content, including tracks generated through AI platforms.

“Content providers will be required to include AI Transparency Tags in any instance where AI was used to create a material portion of the content, including tracks that are AI platform generated. We define AI-platform-generated content as anything that is primarily derived from a generative AI service.” — Apple Music, in an email to industry partners

articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
For the second time this week, an unreleased Apple product has been leaked in shockingly thorough fashion. After a video demonstrating camera-equipped AirPods was spotted in macOS 26.7 on Monday, the Beats 360 over-ears headphones have now been revealed on multiple retail websites despite not yet officially existing.

The headphones were spotted by Redditors on Amazon U.K., and one user going by the handle HappyMcPe promptly started a thread featuring more than half a dozen photos of the device. They were also spotted on other retail sites such as Apcom Slovakia and Misco, but all the listings now appear to have been taken down.

Based on the images–which we would tend to assume are legitimate, since they were used by multiple legitimate retailers and have been guiltily taken down since being spotted–the new headphones have a noticeably different design from the two currently available Beats over-ears. Unlike the Studio Pro and Solo 4, the Beats 360 has a separate padded section on the underside of the headpiece, as well as much more of an open mesh on the earcups.

Elsewhere in the listings it’s made clear that the padded section can be detached, as can the cushions over the ears, and that these are available separately as an Extra Cushion Kit. There seems to be two versions of the cushion: Performance Knit and UltraPlush.

The images also make it apparent that these are the same unreleased headphones which football star Lamine Yamal was seen with in multiple Instagram posts earlier this summer.

While we’re discussing design, it’s worth mentioning that the color finishes are very MacBook Neo-coded. The 360 is available in Sky, Black, Navy, Cloud, Pink, and Volt (a bright neon yellow and a good match for the Neo’s Citrus finish). That’s way more options, incidentally, than the Studio Pro, which comes in four colors, or the Solo 4, which comes in three.

But the leak spills far more beans than simply what the new headphones look like. We’ve got pricing, for example: £331.99 on Misco, and $299 in the DataVision listing.

In fact, product descriptions reveal almost everything about the new headphones. They offer active noise cancellation (“up to 1. 75x more noise cancellation” than the Beats Studio Pro, the description claims), though they don’t appear to feature an H2 or indeed any other Apple chip. They are rated as IPX4 for water and sweat resistance. They’re compatible with both Apple and Android products.

They have all-day battery life even with ANC enabled. They can be folded flat. They come with a “woven ripstop fabric carrying case. ”

It’s another huge leak, in other words. We don’t know when the headphones will come out, but based on the number of retail companies that had the information, we’d guess it’ll be soon. Watch this space in the coming days for any remaining details that weren’t accidentally leaked today.

articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio

articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 Review Roundup: All Hail the Return of MGS4
articles.subtitle: Critics leap at the chance to dig into Guns of the Patriots, one of Hideo Kojima's thorniest and weirdest games Related There's only one thing most reviewers of Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Critics leap at the chance to dig into Guns of the Patriots, one of Hideo Kojima's thorniest and weirdest games

Related

There's only one thing most reviewers of Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 care about, and that's the return to playability of Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. Perhaps the strangest, most personal, and most divisive game Hideo Kojima has made, the 2008 epic has been stuck on PlayStation 3 with no compatibility with modern consoles, unlike the rest of the Solid Snake saga.

Although reviewers find plenty to criticize in the game, including its self-indulgence and overreliance on extremely long cutscenes, they agree that it's a fascinating and prescient title that's well worth revisiting — and that the 4K, 60 frames per second presentation of the new remaster is a big improvement on the original. These factors, and just the pleasure of having the game available to play again, contribute to a strong rating of 85 on Metacritic and 84 on OpenCritic.

Polygon's Giovanni Colantonio highlights the historical importance of Metal Gear Solid 4, and how increasingly rare it is to find any game, let alone a big-budget one, that will reckon with video games' complicated and complicit relationship with war. " Metal Gear Solid Master Collection: Vol. 2 is the year’s most necessary game release," Colantonio writes.

"It’s a rebuttal to the myth that video games have become more outwardly progressive in recent years; its long admonishments about countries that profit off of war are fiercer than anything you’ll find in a big-budget game this year. [. . . ] As deeply imperfect as Metal Gear Solid 4 is today, it’s a reminder of how much ground video game publishers have ceded to the war machine.

It's an anti-war protest marching into captured territory. "

"I’m immensely grateful to have experienced it, and I will probably never play it again," writes Kotaku's Cole Kronman in his critical deep dive. For Kronman, the game is most interesting as Kojima's metafictional and somewhat ambivalent reckoning with the series he created. "To play it is to see a frustrated artist’s messy contention with his own work and audience unfold in real time. It is, among everything else, deeply, jarringly human."

PC Gamer's Morgan Park focuses on Metal Gear Solid 4 's mechanics and where it sits in the evolution of stealth games, as a once vital genre was being subsumed by straight-up action gaming. "Playing it today, the particular way it mixes mercurial stealth and heavy weaponry is anything but routine," Park writes.

"OId Snake skulks through active battlefields, bewildered by the growing mundanity of war, as Kojima grapples with the undeniable appeal of getting in the shit. This is a stealth game that doesn't mind if you try to play it like Call of Duty, but going loud comes at the cost of stressing Snake the fuck out. "

But Guns of the Patriots isn't the only game in this collection, as VGC's Jordan Middler reminds us. "Come for Metal Gear Solid 4, stay for two handheld classics," Middler says, referring to the PSP game Metal Gear Solid 4: Peace Walker and the Game Boy's Metal Gear: Ghost Babel, an alternate-history retelling of the first Metal Gear Solid.

"[ Ghost Babel ] received huge critical praise when it was first released, though it’s an entry that many may have missed," MIddler writes. "This collection marks the first time it’s ever been rereleased. Similar to Peace Walker, if you’re a player who only ever delved into the console side of the Metal Gear franchise, you’re missing the entire picture. "

Recommended For You

Reviewers note that Konami's remastering work on the collection is simple but effective, and the games play well. Other than that, they don't spend a lot of time on the collection itself, perhaps because its presentation is so bare-bones. "It feels like this side of the collection could really have done with a little more care and attention," writes Push Square's John Cal McCormick.

"Yes, the main draw here is Metal Gear Solid 4 on PS5, and once you get into the games the presentation of the collection is long forgotten, but it would still have been nice to see something that felt a little less thrown together. "

But almost every review agrees that the return of Metal Gear Solid 4 is, as Kronman says, a "historic moment for game preservation." You can celebrate it yourself when Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is released on Aug. 27.

Apple rarely confirms event dates far in advance, and there’s no guarantee an event will take place within its usual window. That leaves Apple fans – and anyone considering a new Apple device – wondering when the next Apple event will happen and what might be announced.

Luckily, Apple’s annual schedule is predictable, giving us a good idea of when the next keynote will happen – and which products are likely to launch. Based on Apple’s long-established schedule and reliable rumours, we can make informed estimates about when the next keynote is likely and which products could headline it.

From the iPhone 18 lineup and new Apple Watches to potential Mac and iPad updates, here’s everything we know about Apple’s next event and what you can expect to see. Read on for a closer look at all of the events Apple is expected to hold in 2026 and beyond, and what could launch.

When is Apple’s next event?

Apple still hasn’t made an official announcement about the date

Beginning of September (expected)

Apple has not yet announced the date of its next event, although the company has asked Apple Store staff to apply for the ” Event Support Experience Program.” Employees enter a lottery for the opportunity to assist with an Apple event scheduled for the first half of September.

articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

When Tramell Tillman was first cast in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, fans speculated wildly about who the Severance star might be playing in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Was he Norman Osborn? A recast version of Kang the Conqueror? Something called Spider-Slayer? Nobody knew — not even Tillman's closest friends and family.

"I didn't tell anybody that I was a part of Spider-Man until the news was released," the actor reveals to Polygon. "I remember it was in August of 2025, when the news was announced, and everyone was asking me who I was playing, and I said, 'I cannot tell you. I am so sorry.'"

A full year later, the secret is out. Seemingly everyone on the planet has now seen Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which means Tillman is finally free to discuss everything about the movie, from his own character Bill Metzger's motivations to some of its biggest twists, turns, and character reveals. Polygon recently caught up with Tillman over Zoom to ask him our eight most pressing questions about Brand New Day. Check out his answers below.

Warning: There are huge, Hulk-sized spoilers for the entire plot of Spider-Man: Brand New Day in this article.

1 Was Bill Metzger justified in what he did to Jean Grey?

Let's cut right to the chase: In Brand New Day, Tillman's character, Bill Metzger, is the head of the Department of Damage Control. Early on, he partners with Spider-Man (Tom Holland) to stop a powerful psychic villain who later turns out to be Jean Grey (Sadie Sink). By the end of the film, we learn that Metzger had previously kidnapped Jean's sister (who also had psychic powers) and performed brutal experiments on her until she died. He then captures Jean and attempts to do the same thing.

He did what he needed to do to protect people.

Pretty evil stuff, but Jean is also a serious threat in the movie who puts thousands of lives at risk and seemingly kills at least one innocent person. (Plus she's super mean to Peter.) So is Metzger's attempt to control Jean and her powers justified? Tillman won't go that far, but he empathizes with his character.

"I think what he did was motivated by his desire to protect the people he served," the actor says. "He knew there was a threat out there, and it's a very dangerous threat, and he needed to get to the bottom of it. He's the type of person to do what he needs to do in order to protect or preserve the greater good. He did what he needed to do to protect people."

2 Where is Metzger now?

The final confrontation between Spider-Man, Jean Grey, and Metzger resolves suddenly when Punisher (Jon Bernthal) accidentally shoots Spidey with a sniper rifle. The movie then cuts to a hospital, leaving Metzger's fate uncertain, although it's implied he managed to escape. So where is the character now?

"He's on the apology tour," Tillman says with a laugh, before offering a more realistic answer. "I don't know. Probably taking a vacation. He encountered some pretty heavy stuff. I remember having this conversation with [director] Destin [Daniel Cretton] and Justin [Kuritzkes], the writer that I was working with. We were talking about what it would be like to experience power like Jean Grey.

And as a result of the experimentation that he was doing on Jean, it intensified. Metzger got a front row seat to experience that. So I imagine he's probably hiding out somewhere trying to recoup. Because that's intense. Like near death. The glass was right in his eyes. He probably thought he was going to die. "

3 What did Justin Kuritzkes bring to Brand New Day 's script?

Brand New Day was co-written by Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers, the screenwriting duo behind the previous three Spider-Man movies. However, for this one, Sony also brought in Justin Kuritzkes ( Challengers ) to help director Destin Daniel Cretton on re-writes. Tillman worked directly with Kuritzkes to give his character more depth.

We both liked the idea that he was married.

"We talked a little about Metzger's backstory," Tillman says. "We both liked the idea that he was married. Him having a family is what helped raise the stakes. I'm not going to use the word justified, but anybody who has a significant other or kids, you move differently through the world because there's people you love, and you care about relying on you. That helped to really lock him in; to push him forward. Those little details helped to make the character more full and well-rounded, if you will.

articles.title: WhatCable Reports on USB-C Cable Power and Speed
articles.subtitle: Most of us probably have a collection of random USB-C cables that have arrived over the years with various devices and peripherals or were purchased quickly as needed.
articles.author: TidBITS
articles.content:
Most of us probably have a collection of random USB-C cables that have arrived over the years with various devices and peripherals or were purchased quickly as needed. Apart from the difference between smooth and braided cables and the colors—most of mine are either white or black—they’re nearly impossible to tell apart.

Someone who is more obsessive than I might have labeled them when they arrived, but I suspect most people just toss them in a drawer, box, or bag. I’ll show you mine if you show me yours (yes, I still keep some things in 3. 5-inch floppy boxes).

But not all USB-C cables are created equal. Even beyond the difference between Thunderbolt and USB, USB-C cables can support a wide variety of power and bandwidth specs. For instance, Apple is notorious for shipping “charge-only” cables that support data only at slow USB 2.0 speeds of 480 Mbps. And there’s no way to know what the random cable that shipped alongside some device can do.

Hardware testers exist—some of my Apple Consultants Network friends carry this Treedix USB Cable Tester —but for most people, they’re overkill. Instead, download the WhatCable app, which gives you a vast amount of information about your cables for free. A paid WhatCable Pro tier ($13.99/£9.99) lets you name cables and shows what each port, cable, and device combination can do and has negotiated.

Using WhatCable is trivially easy—you just launch the app and scroll through its reports on each cable/device that’s attached via USB-C. It shows you the port in use, the cable type in bold (Thunderbolt / USB4 in this case), a brief description of what the cable can do, and boxed summaries of the cable’s capabilities for charging, throughput, and display quality.

After that, it lists all the details it can discern about the cable and what it knows about the connected devices (an Apple Studio Display in this case). If you’re a glutton for technical punishment (“please sir, more specs! ”), click the Show Technical Details switch at the bottom.

Those Apple “charge-only” cables? They look a lot different in WhatCable, as you can see from this one connecting my iPhone 17 to my Mac. You really don’t want to use one of these cables to connect an external SSD.

In this case, it doesn’t matter what cable I use because the iPhone 17 itself is limited to 480 Mbps. That became obvious when I switched to my go-to OWC Thunderbolt 4 cable. Even though WhatCable correctly identifies it as a Thunderbolt cable capable of 40 Gbps, the app notes that only USB 2.0 is active because of the iPhone 17’s limitations.

It was also illustrative to plug in an Anker USB-C hub with several USB-A ports and then attach an old OWC hard drive that turned out to be limited to USB 2.0’s 480 Mbps and a SanDisk flash drive that supported USB 3.0’s 5 Gbps. I wouldn’t have guessed the hard drive was that slow just from looking at it.

I could keep working my way through the rat’s nest of USB-C cables in that bag, but you get the idea. WhatCable also includes macOS widgets so you can see what’s connected at a glance and can trigger notifications when cables connect or disconnect. You can choose between a normal windowed app or a menu bar popover, and Terminal wonks can even run it at the command line.

As long as you’re running a Mac with Apple silicon running macOS 14 Sonoma or later (Intel-based Macs are out of luck), I encourage you to download WhatCable 1.4 today and take a spin through its documentation for more details. If you regularly work with many USB-C cables, consider WhatCable Pro for its additional identification and diagnostic capabilities.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: 5 Nintendo Games You Need to Play at Least Once
articles.subtitle: Some of the most pivotal games in Nintendo's modern history Nintendo 's reputation for decades of certified bangers is well-earned, though between new releases and the classics that hog all the attention, it's easy to overlook some of the company's more...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Some of the most pivotal games in Nintendo's modern history

Nintendo 's reputation for decades of certified bangers is well-earned, though between new releases and the classics that hog all the attention, it's easy to overlook some of the company's more influential games. Maybe you're young and missed out on entire generations of essential games, or you're (comparatively) old, like me, and got into video games later in life. Whatever the case, learning about them through cultural osmosis isn't quite the same as playing them yourself.

I'm not gonna tell you to go play Super Mario Bros. 3 or A Link to the Past. You should play them, but you've probably heard that from a dozen other people already.

This list is more interested in examining a few pivotal games from Nintendo's history that marked turning points for the company, either for the risk involved in making them or by representing a high point in creative design that informed Nintendo's future strategies.

All of these are available in some form or another on modern hardware, either via remakes, Nintendo Switch Online 's retro library, or even on PC thanks to later ports.

5 Metroid Prime (Remastered on Nintendo Switch)

Metroid Prime 's a bit of an obvious choice given its popularity, but it's no less deserving of a recommendation. It was a big, potentially risky step forward, a bid to make an obsolete franchise relevant again, and Nintendo adopting a genre that its competitors had dominated in that generation. The gambit paid off spectacularly.

Metroid Prime is an exceptional case study in level design and integrating storytelling and puzzles in a type of interactive media that's usually hostile to those things. In other words, it proved FPS games can be smart and shoot-y at the same time without sacrificing anything.

It also set a precedent for how Nintendo would approach its other lagging franchises in later years, like Donkey Kong Bananza and Breath of the Wild — redefining them with big creative leaps that defied expectations.

4 Pikmin (Gamecube, NSO)

Nintendo played it safe with the GameCube. You might think otherwise, what with Mario Sunshine sending the plumber on a goop-cleaning vacation and The Wind Waker turning Link and Zelda into cartoons. These were still Mario and Zelda games, though. And what is Luigi's Mansion, but a Mario is Missing that doesn't suck?

Pikmin was something new and wildly different than anything Nintendo had developed for years: A real-time strategy game (a genre that, nearly three decades later, remains quite niche) starring a corporate lackey and an army of sentient, expendable vegetables.

The idea is that the lackey crashed on an alien planet and needs to rebuild his ship, which he can't do alone because everything is gigantic. And he has 30 days before he dies. That's where the sentient veggies come in, to lend a… well, whatever they use in place of hands, by finding and grabbing ship parts and avoiding the murderous indigenous fauna in the process.

It's a giant puzzle with a timer, basically, and it makes you feel really, really bad when one of your veggie friends dies. It also features some of Nintendo's best level design, the kind of work that makes me wish the company developed more puzzle games.

Recommended For You

3 Fire Emblem (Game Boy Advance, NSO)

If you liked Three Houses and are excited about Fortune's Weave, you can thank Fire Emblem: The Blazing Blade (just plain Fire Emblem for everywhere outside Japan). It's the seventh Fire Emblem game and the first that Nintendo launched internationally, after years of assuming the series' difficulty would alienate American and European audiences. Maybe it would have.

Intelligent Systems found success with Advance Wars a few years before, but that was a different story. Your COs can't die, for one thing, and (on some maps) you can always rebuild units. Fire Emblem 's permadeath and lengthy, large-scale tactical battles were a different matter, but Nintendo wanted to make this one of its major franchises.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

The Apple Developer YouTube channel shared an interesting 90-minute WWDC26 session today called “ Inside Apple Intelligence and Xcode: Special Presentation. ”

While parts of the presentation can get technical, after all, this is a WWDC session, the video offers very interesting insight into what developers will be able to build using the new technologies, frameworks, and APIs it announced during the event.

Perhaps one of the more interesting parts of the video is a 20-minute segment in which an entire app is built from a single prompt and then further tweaked with follow-up commands.

articles.title: Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots review
articles.subtitle: The new best way to play Kojima's strangest sequel.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
What is it A re-release of Solid Snake's legendary final mission. Release date August 27, 2026 Expect to pay $50/£40 Publisher Konami Developer Kojima Productions, Konami Reviewed on RTX 5090, Ryzen 7 9800X3D 4.7 GHz, 64GB RAM & Steam Deck Multiplayer None Steam Deck Verified Link Official site

Stealth has changed.

It's no longer about avoidance, visibility, or tension. It's an endless series of "stealth action" games trivializing the uncertainty of sneaking and pushing players into open conflict. The age of camouflage has become the age of tall grass: stealth is no longer treated as a genre worthy of big budgets, but an optional feature of conventional action games. [Takes a long drag from a cigarette] Stealth has changed. And when the player's visibility is under total control… espionage becomes routine.

Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots was at the vanguard of the stealth action shift in 2008—but playing it today, the particular way it mixes mercurial stealth and heavy weaponry is anything but routine. Snake is outfitted with a tranq pistol, non-lethal CQC training, and the latest OctoCamo sneaking suit, an ingenious invention of espionage that automatically camouflages the user to their surroundings.

In his other pocket are enough guns to arm a strike force—SMGs, shotguns, ARs, RPGs, a rail gun—customizable with Create-a-Class attachments.

OId Snake skulks through active battlefields, bewildered by the growing mundanity of war, as Kojima grapples with the undeniable appeal of getting in the shit. This is a stealth game that doesn't mind if you try to play it like Call of Duty, but going loud comes at the cost of stressing Snake the fuck out.

This Master Collection port, solid alone or alongside Peace Walker, is a genuinely thrilling object: proof that MGS4 wasn't a mass hallucination we all had in 2008, but a uniquely strange meditation on existential anxiety—of warmongering doomerism, automation, desensitized violence, and back pain—trapped for 18 years on a PlayStation 3. Konami has done good work here, though at times the bare minimum: you can now play MGS4 at 4K (yay!), but at a locked 60 fps (less yay).

Still, that's a lot better than the extremely unreliable 30 fps it once struggled to maintain, and the Master Collection launcher is less cumbersome now than when Volume 1 arrived on PC in 2023. Guns of the Patriots has gone so ignored for so long that it's hard to split hairs here—this is the new best way to play one of my favorites.

Naked sun

Man does it feel great to see Guns of the Patriots cleaned up. It's a special one for me: MGS4 landed just as I reached the age to enjoy games on a deeper level. It was also my first Metal Gear, which is a little hilarious in hindsight, given how obsessed the story is with its own past.

In 2026 I'm seriously charmed by the 2008-ness of this world: from the fully functional iPod (still intact here, but lacking Konami's official Metal Gear hype podcasts) to Kojima's infatuation with the XM8 and P90 (objectively the coolest guns ever made).

Hindsight hasn't done wonders for its meandering plot and sometimes dull cutscenes, but Kojima's vision for a world consumed by greed and accelerated by decision-making AIs is uncomfortably spot-on. More than anything else though, MGS4's long exile has given me a new appreciation for its extremely balanced stealth.

Acts 1 and 2—where MGS4 really flexes its sneaking muscles—are the sort of triumphant stealth sandboxes that are quite rare these days. Maps are focused and linear, but brimming with options. Guards are reactive, consistent, emotive, and learnable. The years have gifted me patience for stillness, and MGS4 is most fun at a snail's pace.

Slithering between guards six inches away from their boots camouflaged as a patch of dirt is a bigger thrill than crouching through tall grass in Horizon, Ghost of Tsushima, or any modern Assassin's Creed.

I love that Kojima can't help but hand players a box of toys with hidden functions. I'm always picking up three times more gear than I'll ever use, which I've learned is a blessing, because every replay is an opportunity to get fixated on a tool. This time, I finally learned how useful Playboy magazines can be when you're trying to ghost an area.

This is also the playthrough in which I remembered that the Mark 2 robot, a drivable drone with a cloak and stun prod, is very useful for covertly retrieving items in risky locations.

Tactical espionage action

Replaying Guns of the Patriots and Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory in the same year is highlighting just how bland open worlds have made level design. I love MGS5, but its small Far Cry villages that have to be approachable from all angles are trounced by MGS4's busy battlefields. My favorite is the Act 2 raid on Liquid's mansion, where Snake has to bypass several active warzones either by choosing a side or concealing himself in the chaos.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: There Will Never Be Another Game Like Metal Gear Solid 4
articles.subtitle: Video games have changed Midway through Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots, just as Solid Snake is about to ride into a high-octane motorcycle shootout, director Hideo Kojima forces players to have a come-to-Jesus moment.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Video games have changed

Midway through Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots, just as Solid Snake is about to ride into a high-octane motorcycle shootout, director Hideo Kojima forces players to have a come-to-Jesus moment. Big Mama stops to explain that her troops are child soldiers. They’re largely orphans who grew up surrounded by warfare.

They started working in the arms industry, and moved to combat as a way to support their younger siblings while getting revenge on the companies responsible for killing their parents. The dystopian monologue is capped off by a sobering reality check.

“Nowadays, anyone with a computer can get combat training,” Big Mama says. “The FPS games these children love are distributed for free by these companies. Of course, it’s all just virtual training. It’s so easy for them to get absorbed by these war games. And before they know it, they’re in the PMCs holding real guns. These kids end up fighting in proxy wars that have nothing to do with their own lives. They think it’s cool to fight like this. They think combat is life.”

18 years later, when Metal Gear Solid 4 is now old enough to buy cigarettes and be recruited for military service, that monologue is more prescient than ever. And you can finally revisit it thanks to Metal Gear Solid Master Collection: Vol. 2, which brings the PlayStation 3 game to Windows PC and modern consoles for the first time, alongside Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker and Metal Gear: Ghost Babel.

It’s an important moment for video game preservation, especially in the wake of the PS3 store’s recent shutdown, but it’s also a reminder of a dark truth: It’s impossible to imagine a game like Metal Gear Solid 4 ever existing again.

Set five years after Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty, Guns of the Patriots plays like a 15-hour anxiety spiral. Everything Solid Snake was fighting to stop has come to pass. Senseless war has broken out around the world, made all the more deadly by mech warriors who now roam the Middle East gunning down rival PMC soldiers.

Now on the verge of death due to the effects of accelerated aging, Solid Snake sets out on one last globe-trotting mission to unmask a global conspiracy, destroy the AI that powers it, and put an end to the age of war.

Despite critics hailing it as Kojima’s magnum opus in 2008, it was a polarizing release. Its abundance of long-winded cutscenes (including a record-setting 70-minute finale! ) drew criticism from players who felt like Kojima seemed more interested in making movies than games.

The release won’t do much to change players' opinions, even if it's dropping at a time when cinematic storytelling is all the rage in games. It’s still a largely hands-off experience that’s invested in tying up every single loose thread in the series. Call it fan service or payoff, but it’s still impressive to witness it and feel like every single detail in the series’ history was placed there for a reason.

Perhaps what’s changed most with age is that the cutscenes are now a reprieve from the gameplay. Metal Gear Solid 4 is hard to get through in 2026, and Master Collection: Vol. 2 doesn’t try to rewrite history.

Every wart is preserved in a faithful remaster (aside from a new voice line to account for the fact that you no longer need to switch discs midway through it) filled with agonizing boss fights, dull tailing missions, and unwieldy third-person shooting.

Aside from its strong opening chapter, where Snake navigates the streets of an unnamed Middle Eastern city like a deadly maze, Metal Gear Solid 4 is the series’ messiest game in retrospect.

But the poorly aged stealth action is far from the most shocking thing about Metal Gear Solid 4. Instead, it’s how direct Kojima is about tackling political issues without mincing a single word. Developed in the midst of the War on Terror, Metal Gear Solid 4 acts as an indictment of the entire military industrial complex. It isn’t subtle about its commentary either.

“The age of difference has become the age of control, all in the name of averting catastrophe from weapons of mass destruction,” Snake says in a particularly pointed opening monologue.

In 2008, musings like this had a clear target. Metal Gear Solid 4 was largely developed during the waning years of George W. Bush’s presidency, after it had come to light that his administration lied about Iraq possessing WMDs in order to justify a continued war effort. It became a global issue as the United States roped in allies to fight in a never-ending war where the mission was always changing.

Though Kojima isn’t an American, his series had become inextricable from American politics. Don’t forget that Metal Gear Solid 2, a game about terrorism largely set in New York City, launched just two months after September 11.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.subtitle: One is a chaotic 200-player World War I shooter, while the other is a tactical RPG built around customizable mechs Related Steam regularly gives PC players a chance to try something new without spending a cent, whether through games that are temporarily free...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
One is a chaotic 200-player World War I shooter, while the other is a tactical RPG built around customizable mechs

Related

Steam regularly gives PC players a chance to try something new without spending a cent, whether through games that are temporarily free to play or occasional giveaways that can be kept forever. These promotions can be a good excuse to sample a lesser-known game you might otherwise overlook, or convince a few friends to dedicate a weekend to a new multiplayer experience.

Two very different games with positive reviews are currently getting the free-to-play treatment, and you have until Aug. 4 to give them a go. Neither is free to keep, so access disappears once the promotional period ends, though both games are also discounted for anyone who decides to stick around.

Chaotic 200-player battles set in World War I

The first game, Over The Top: WWI, is a large-scale World War I shooter that launched in March 2026. Its huge battles invite some obvious comparisons to modern war games like Battlefield 6 and Hell Let Loose, with infantry fighting alongside tanks, artillery, and aircraft across maps that can support as many as 200 players.

It's rougher around the edges and less cinematic than mainstream warfare titles, but that lack of polish is part of the appeal: explosions can tear apart fortifications and reshape the battlefield, while players can dig trenches and build up defensive positions as a match unfolds.

The free weekend arrives alongside the game's new US Expeditionary Forces update, which adds the United States to the conflict along with new maps, uniforms, weapons, vehicles, and a first-person perspective.

A remake of a PlayStation tactical RPG classic

The other free-to-play game is Front Mission 3: Remake, a turn-based tactical RPG built around battles between heavily customizable mechs known as Wanzers. Released on Steam in January, it's a modern remake of the 1999 PlayStation game, with updated graphics and animations, reorchestrated music, and a new quick combat mode.

Rather than the huge multiplayer firefights of Over The Top: WWI, Front Mission 3 is a slower, more methodical strategy game. Players take control of Kazuki Takemura and his squad as they become embroiled in a military conspiracy involving corporations, secret weapons, and competing nations. Battles revolve around positioning and customizing individual Wanzer parts and weapons, making it a particularly good fit for players who like mechs, JRPGs, and turn-based strategy games.

Both games are free to play on Steam for a limited time, so this is an easy chance to try something outside your usual rotation without committing to a purchase. If either one clicks, the temporary discounts make it cheaper to keep playing once the free period ends.
